Al Wajh (port locode SAWAJ ), aka Al Wejh/Wedjh, is a Red Sea cruise port and city in Saudi Arabia's Tabuk Province, with population around 50,000. The city is inhabited mainly by Saudis and the economy is largely based on commercial fishing.

Al Wajh Airport (1984-established) serves exclusively domestic flights (by the national carrier Saudia) linking with Jeddah (Saudi Arabia's largest seaport) and Riyadh (the country's capital city).

In April 2021, MSC and Cruise Saudi (fully-owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund) announced a partnership for launching Red Sea cruises (2021-2022 winter season) with the homeporting in Jeddah of the ship MSC Magnifica.

  • Magnifica was scheduled to operate 7-day voyages (November 2021 through March 2022) visiting 3 Saudi ports - including weekly calls to Port Al-Wajh (gateway to the UNESCO site Hegra in Al-Ula).
  • In addition to Magnifica's itineraries, MSC Virtuosa had scheduled Arabian Gulf 2021 winter program (December 2021 through March 2022) with visits to Prot Dammam and the Al-Ahsa Oasis.
  • With the two MSC liners, Cruise Saudi expected ~170,000 tourists during season 2021-2022.
  • MSC's Saudi Arabia voyages were also offered as fly-cruise deals with fares inclusive of direct flights between Europe and Jeddah (King Abdulaziz Airport) provided by Saudia (fka Saudi Arabian Airlines). As part of the agreement, Saudia's flight schedules were modified to fit the two MSC cruise ships' homeport times (departure and arrival).

Al Wajh is a small Red Sea port where the most practical local sightseeing is the historic waterfront district rather than a long list of major attractions. The old town preserves coral-stone buildings, traditional wooden rawasheen windows, historic mosques and a compact harbor setting. Al Wajh is also promoted as a maritime gateway to Hegra and AlUla, but those sites require a substantial inland transfer.

At a Glance

  • Independent sightseeing: Independent with some planning or transport.
  • Best independent option: Old Al Wajh, the historic harbor and Corniche.
  • Port access: Al Wajh is an emerging cruise destination without the established passenger-terminal infrastructure found at major Saudi ports. Cruise calls may use tenders into the working harbor; passengers should follow their ship's instructions for the actual landing point.
  • Getting around: The historic district itself is compact, but local public transport is limited and taxis should not be assumed to be waiting at the cruise landing.
  • Major excursion: Hegra and AlUla are possible only on sufficiently long calls and are much better suited to organized excursions.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Do not assume the CruiseMapper map pin is the exact passenger exit. Al Wajh's harbor is primarily a working maritime and fishing area, and cruise landing arrangements can vary between ships and seasons. Larger ships have generally used tender operations rather than a conventional cruise pier.

If your ship provides transport to the historic waterfront or Al Balad, independent exploration from that drop-off is straightforward. Without a transfer, pre-arranged transport is preferable to relying on a taxi appearing at the harbor. There is no well-established tourist bus network for moving cruise passengers around Al Wajh.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Explore Old Al Wajh and the Historic Harbor

Allow about 2–3 hours. This is the best choice for passengers who want to see Al Wajh itself. Walk through the Al Balad historic quarter to see traditional Red Sea architecture, including limestone and coral-stone buildings, wooden balconies and rawasheen screens. The lanes lead naturally toward the old harbor, historic mosques and Al Wajh Castle.

The area is best appreciated on foot once you have reached the old town. Some heritage buildings are fragile or unrestored, so treat them as exterior sights unless access is clearly permitted.

Walk the Corniche and Waterfront

Allow about 1–2 hours. Al Wajh has a long developed waterfront, including an urban Corniche of about 2 km (1.2 mi). It is suitable for an easy sea-view walk and can be combined with the old town rather than treated as a separate excursion.

Much of the wider waterfront extends well beyond the historic center, so there is little reason for cruise passengers to walk its full length. Shade can be limited, making shorter sections more practical in warm weather.

Visit Zurayb Castle

Allow about 2–3 hours including transport. Zurayb Castle stands approximately 10 km (6.2 mi) east of Al Wajh. The restored historic fortress was associated with the Egyptian pilgrimage route and contains defensive towers, a central courtyard and internal rooms.

This is not a walking excursion from the port. Arrange a vehicle in advance and preferably keep the same driver for the return, as finding onward transport at an outlying heritage site may be difficult.

Hegra and AlUla

Organized excursion recommended. Cruise lines have marketed Al Wajh as a gateway to Hegra, Saudi Arabia's UNESCO-listed Nabataean site. Hegra is roughly 200 km (124.3 mi) inland by road, with transfers commonly taking around 2.5–3 hours each way depending on routing and road conditions. AlUla town is farther, at roughly 245 km (152.2 mi) by road.

The journey consumes a large part of the port day, and Hegra visits use controlled visitor arrangements and timed access. Attempting this independently during an ordinary cruise call carries considerably more transport and timing risk than staying in Al Wajh. Consider it only on a long call and preferably through the ship or another fully pre-arranged excursion that coordinates entry and return transport.

Self-Guided Walking Tour: Old Al Wajh

Distance: approximately 2–3 km (1.2–1.9 mi)
Pure walking time: about 40–50 minutes
Recommended total time: 2–3 hours
Difficulty: Easy to moderate. Mostly level, but historic lanes can have uneven surfaces and there may be little shade.

Start: the ship's old-town or waterfront transfer drop-off. Do not begin this route from an unfamiliar industrial or commercial harbor gate unless your cruise line confirms that pedestrian access is permitted.

  1. Old Harbor: Begin beside the historic waterfront for views of the bay and Al Wajh's traditional maritime setting.
  2. Al Balad: Enter the old quarter and explore the compact network of historic streets.
  3. Traditional Rawasheen Houses: Look for projecting wooden windows, balconies, old doors and coral-stone or limestone construction typical of Red Sea architecture.
  4. Historic Mosques: Pass the old neighborhood mosques and view their simple coastal architecture from the surrounding streets. Respect worshippers and avoid entering unless visitor access is clearly permitted.
  5. Al Wajh Castle: Continue to the historic fort overlooking the old port area. Interior access can vary, so the route remains worthwhile even if only the exterior is open.
  6. Corniche: Finish with a waterfront walk before returning to the agreed ship-transfer or tender meeting point.

The old quarter is compact enough that it is better to wander slowly through the architecture than attempt a long-distance walk. Keep track of the route back to your cruise meeting point, particularly if the tender landing and town drop-off are different locations.

Beaches and Red Sea Nature

The Al Wajh coast borders extensive reefs, lagoons and Red Sea marine habitats, while the developed waterfront stretches for more than 17 km (10.6 mi). For a cruise call, however, independent beach time is less straightforward than the old-town walk because suitable swimming access, transport and return arrangements depend on the specific location.

If your ship offers a beach, snorkeling or boat excursion, it is generally more practical than independently searching for a beach after arrival. Do not assume that every attractive stretch of coastline has public facilities, safe swimming access or transport back to the harbor.

Practical Tips

  • Confirm the tender or docking arrangement on board before planning an independent walk.
  • Pre-arrange transport if you intend to leave central Al Wajh, especially for Zurayb Castle or any coastal destination.
  • Carry water and sun protection; exposed waterfront and heritage areas can have limited shade.
  • Dress modestly, particularly around mosques and traditional neighborhoods.
  • Do not plan Hegra or AlUla independently unless the call is long enough to absorb several hours of road travel in each direction.
  • For tender calls, follow the ship's published last-tender time rather than working only from the scheduled departure time, and allow extra return margin for transport or tender queues.
